title: Why startup success is the journey, not the exit
summary: Using Depeche Mode's Rose Bowl peak as a cautionary tale, Cohen argues that tying success to a single outcome (an exit, a metric, a funding round) almost guarantees failure and unhappiness. Keep score with metrics and money, but make the years of building the point. It also helps recruit people who want to join the journey.

principles.text: Don't define success as one peak moment; the peak means your next steps are downhill, so value the building itself.
principles.quote: The way you let this happen is to believe that the goal is to achieve a single moment of success--a big sale, going public, or passing it on to your daughter.

principles.text: You spend nearly all your time on the journey, so the journey is where happiness has to come from.
principles.quote: You spend 99.99% of your time on the journey of building a startup, and 0.01% basking in the temporary euphoria of "success," such as selling it to someone else or ringing the bell on the morning of your IPO.

principles.text: Outcome-based definitions of success (metrics, money, exits, funding) almost guarantee failure by your own definition.
principles.quote: But if your measure of "success" is based on a specific outcome--based on metrics, or money, or growth-rate, or number of employees, or whether you had an exit, or how much money you raised

principles.text: Keep score with metrics and money, but don't confuse the game with life.
principles.quote: Keep score, so long as you can distinguish between the game and life.

principles.text: Valuing the journey helps hiring: later employees join to be part of the journey, not just for early-stage upside.
principles.quote: the first employee joins because it's the ground floor of an exciting startup, but why will the 20th person join? Or the 200th?
